analysis.one_liner: Bars drug-pricing middlemen from hiding rebates and markups in the federal employee health plan.
analysis.headline: A bill to force pharmacy benefit managers to open their books for the federal employee health plan sat in committee for nearly two years and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: H.R. 1367 targeted the middlemen that manage drug benefits for the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program (FEHBP) — the health plan covering roughly 8 million federal employees, retirees, and their families. It would have required carriers and their pharmacy benefit managers to disclose to the Office of Personnel Management the true net cost of drugs, including rebates and discounts, and to give OPM full access to their contract information, with penalties — including False Claims Act liability — for overcharges billed to the government. Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-MA) introduced it on March 21, 2013. It was referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
analysis.who_benefits: The millions of federal employees, retirees, and dependents enrolled in FEHBP, who pay part of their drug costs through premiums and copays, plus taxpayers, who pick up the government's share of premiums. If pharmacy benefit managers had to reveal rebates, discounts, and the spread between what the plan pays and what pharmacies are reimbursed, overcharges would be visible and recoverable, lowering drug costs for the plan. Independent pharmacies also stood to benefit from limits on hidden pricing spreads.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibited OPM from contracting with or approving FEHBP carriers whose pharmacy benefit manager arrangements did not meet its disclosure requirements, forcing pricing middlemen to open their books.

It required carriers to disclose the net cost of drugs — the final cost after rebates, discounts, and other price adjustments — so the plan could see what drugs actually cost rather than a marked-up list price.

It gave the Office of Personnel Management full access to information about contracts entered into by pharmacy benefit managers, and defined acquisition cost (what a pharmacy actually pays) versus allowable cost (what the PBM sets), exposing spread pricing.

It attached penalties for overcharges, including liability for claims submitted to the United States Government under the False Claims Act, giving the plan a way to claw back money from middlemen who inflated prices.
It applied to the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, the plan covering federal workers and retirees, so any savings would flow to enrollees' premiums and copays and to the federal budget.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers, the companies that negotiate drug prices and administer pharmacy benefits, would lose revenue from undisclosed rebates and spread pricing — the gap between what a plan pays and what pharmacies are reimbursed. FEHBP carriers would face compliance costs from the new disclosure and audit obligations, some of which could be passed into premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and health carriers

drawbacks.text: The bill covered only the federal employee health plan, not Medicare, Medicaid, or private employer insurance, so its savings would reach a narrow slice of drug spending even if it worked as designed.

Mandatory disclosure of contract terms, rebates, and acquisition costs would impose compliance costs on carriers and PBMs, and some of those costs could be passed into premiums; opponents of transparency mandates also argue that revealing negotiated contract terms can weaken a negotiator's leverage with drug manufacturers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential gains are real but modest in national terms: FEHBP is a large program, so even a few percent off drug costs would mean substantial savings for enrollees and taxpayers. The costs — compliance and possible premium pass-through — are small relative to the overcharges the bill was designed to expose. The main weakness is design scope: it fixes the problem only for one government plan instead of setting a transparency standard for the whole market.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee on the day it was introduced and never came up again — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-MA) introduced the bill on March 21, 2013, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.
Three House members cosponsored the bill, all Democrats.
The complete action record shows no further activity after the referral: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the House.
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and the carriers that profit from undisclosed rebates and spread pricing kept those arrangements untouched, since the bill died before any hearing or vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmacy benefit managers kept hidden pricing intact

for.name: Rep. Stephen F. Lynch
for.role: Sponsor, House Oversight and Government Reform Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require drug-benefit middlemen in the federal employee health plan to disclose rebates, net costs, and contract terms, with penalties for overcharges.

against.name: House Oversight and Government Reform Committee (Chair Darrell Issa, R-OH)
against.what_they_did: The committee of referral never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it remained in committee from March 2013 until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor at any point in the 113th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no party split can be measured; every recorded action on the bill — sponsorship, the three cosponsorships, the committee referral — involved Democrats, and no Republican ever sponsored, cosported, or voted on it.

industries.note: PBMs profit from spread pricing (reimbursing pharmacies less than the plan pays) and from retaining manufacturer rebates without disclosure. The bill targeted exactly those practices, requiring disclosure of net cost and acquisition cost and creating False Claims Act liability for overcharges billed to the government.

Carriers would have had to police their PBM contracts, disclose pricing data to OPM, and accept penalties for overcharges — new compliance costs — but many carriers own PBMs or share in rebate arrangements, so transparency would cut into that revenue too.

Pharmacies are reimbursed by PBMs at an 'allowable cost' the PBM sets, which can be far below what the plan pays; by requiring disclosure of the spread and pharmacy acquisition cost, the bill would pressure PBMs to reimburse pharmacies more fairly.
